vignette:
David speaks about his life’s work with a reverence that has now curdled into something else, something laced with shame. For forty years, he was a journalist, first in Lagos and then in London. He covered coups, civil unrest, and the slow, grinding machinery of politics. His trade was to bear witness, to assemble disjointed facts into a coherent narrative, and to remain steady while the world around him fractured. He believed, with an almost religious conviction, in the power of observation. That was before the night, eighteen months ago, when he was forced to observe and could do nothing.

It was a Tuesday. He and his wife, Funke, were reading in the living room, the quiet punctuated only by the turning of pages and the distant hum of city traffic. The sound that broke the peace wasn't a gunshot or a bomb, the familiar sounds from his past assignments, but the sharp, intimate crack of his own front door splintering. Before he could fully rise from his armchair, two figures were there, faces obscured by balaclavas. He, the man who had stared down soldiers and interviewed warlords, was frozen. One of them pressed something cold and hard against his temple and pushed him back into his chair. The other went for Funke.

He doesn’t talk about what they did to her. His words, once his greatest tool, fail him here. He speaks instead of the details his journalistic mind cataloged against his will: the scuff marks on the intruders' trainers, the faint smell of petrol on one of their jackets, the way the living room lamp cast a long, distorted shadow of his wife’s struggle on the wall. He remembers the silence that followed their departure, a silence so heavy it felt like a physical weight, broken only by Funke’s ragged breaths. He, the observer, the chronicler, was reduced to a footnote in the most horrific story of his life.

In the months that followed, the world outside his home became a minefield of threats. He’d always been a city man, attuned to its rhythms, but now every siren was an alarm, every shout on the street a prelude to violence. He stopped taking the tube, the press of bodies feeling suffocating. At his newspaper, the stories of crime and conflict that had once been his bread and butter became unbearable. He’d stare at the wire reports, and the words would blur, replaced by the image of that shadow on the wall. He began missing deadlines, then avoiding the office altogether, citing illness. The man who once chased stories across continents now found himself unable to walk to the corner shop.

His home, once a sanctuary, became a prison he was compelled to guard. He installed a security system with cameras he checks obsessively on his phone. Before bed, he has a ritual: checking the door lock three times, the windows twice, walking the perimeter of the ground floor until Funke calls his name in a tired, gentle voice. He knows his vigilance is a performance of a power he didn't have then.

Sleep offers no escape. He often wakes with his heart hammering against his ribs, the metallic smell of the gun a phantom in his nostrils. He lies awake for hours, staring at the ceiling, while Funke sleeps beside him—or pretends to. An invisible wall has grown between them, built of his guilt and her pain. He watches her move through her days with a resilience that he, the supposed protector, cannot fathom and feels he has no right to share. He wants to ask if she’s okay, but the question feels like a colossal hypocrisy. He wasn’t okay. He didn’t keep her okay. So he says nothing, and the silence in their house grows heavier than ever.
